paragraphs.heading: A black iron ore
paragraphs.text: Magnetite is a mineral, one of the oxides of iron, and one of the main iron ores. It is black or brownish-black with a metallic luster. Its Mohs hardness is 5–6, and the streak it leaves is black. Chemists call it iron(II,III) oxide, or more commonly ferrous-ferric oxide.

paragraphs.heading: The mineral that is a magnet
paragraphs.text: Magnetite is attracted to a magnet, and it can be magnetized so that it becomes a permanent magnet itself. Leaving aside extremely rare deposits of native iron, no naturally occurring mineral on Earth is more magnetic. Pieces that are magnetized naturally are called lodestone, and they attract small pieces of iron. That is how ancient peoples first discovered magnetism. Lodestones were also used as an early form of magnetic compass.

paragraphs.heading: Where it turns up
paragraphs.text: Igneous and metamorphic rocks very commonly hold small grains of magnetite. Sedimentary rocks can hold it too, banded iron formations among them, and so can the sediments of lakes and seas. Sometimes beach sand holds large quantities of it. Black sands of this kind turn up in various places. Examples are Lung Kwu Tan in Hong Kong, California, and the west coast of New Zealand's North Island. Where there is enough magnetite, it can be found from an aeromagnetic survey, which uses a magnetometer to measure magnetic intensities.

paragraphs.heading: Two kinds of iron
paragraphs.text: Magnetite's chemical composition is written Fe²⁺(Fe³⁺)₂(O²⁻)₄. This shows that it holds two kinds of iron, called ferrous (divalent) and ferric (trivalent). That mix suggests the mineral crystallized in surroundings with intermediate levels of oxygen. The main details of its structure were worked out in 1915, and it was among the first crystal structures obtained using X-ray diffraction.

paragraphs.heading: A clue to how rocks form
paragraphs.text: Magnetite has been important for understanding the conditions under which rocks form. It reacts with oxygen to make hematite. Together the two minerals form a buffer, a pair that can control how oxidizing its environment is. That quantity is called the oxygen fugacity, and the pair is known as the hematite-magnetite or HM buffer. At lower oxygen levels, magnetite can form another buffer with quartz and fayalite, called the QFM buffer. Most igneous rocks have an oxygen fugacity close to the one the QFM buffer produces.

paragraphs.heading: A record of Earth's magnetic field
paragraphs.text: In paleomagnetism, a science that is important for understanding plate tectonics, magnetite has been a critical tool. The ties between magnetite and fellow iron oxide minerals, hematite, ilmenite and ulvospinel among them, have been studied a great deal. How these minerals react with oxygen affects how and when magnetite keeps a record of the Earth's magnetic field.
